title: The Structure of Body Systems
description: A guide to the structure of the skeletal, muscular, cardiovascular and respiratory systems for sport and exercise.
content_html:
Why Body Systems Matter in Sport

Every movement you make in sport — a sprint finish, a tackle, a shot at goal — depends on at least four body systems working in harmony. Sport scientists, physiotherapists and coaches all need a solid understanding of how these systems are structured before they can make sense of how the body responds to exercise. This lesson focuses on the body system structures you are required to know: the skeletal system, the muscular system, the cardiovascular system and the respiratory system.

The Skeletal System

The skeleton is the body's rigid framework. It is made up of 206 bones in an adult and is divided into two main parts: the axial skeleton (skull, vertebral column, ribcage) and the appendicular skeleton (limbs, shoulder girdle, pelvis). Bones are classified by their shape. Long bones — such as the femur, humerus, tibia and fibula — act as levers during movement. Short bones (wrist and ankle bones) provide stability and support. Flat bones — the cranium, scapula, ribs and pelvis — protect vital organs. Irregular bones include the vertebrae of the vertebral column. The main bones you must know are: the cranium (skull), clavicle, scapula, humerus, radius, ulna, ribs, vertebral column, pelvis, femur, patella (kneecap), tibia and fibula.

Key Fact

The main bones you must know are: cranium, scapula, humerus, radius, ulna, ribs, vertebral column, pelvis, femur, patella, tibia and fibula. Work from head to toe and you will not miss any.

Types of Joint and Synovial Joint Structure

Where two or more bones meet, a synovial joint allows free movement. All synovial joints share the same basic structure: a joint capsule encloses the joint, lined by the synovial membrane which secretes synovial fluid to lubricate and nourish the articular cartilage. Articular (hyaline) cartilage covers the ends of bones, reducing friction. Ligaments connect bone to bone, stabilising the joint. The three synovial joint types you need to know are: ball and socket joints (shoulder and hip — allow movement in all planes), hinge joints (knee and elbow — allow flexion and extension only) and pivot joints (top of the vertebral column/atlas and axis — allow rotation).

A synovial joint contains six key structures that work together to allow smooth, pain-free movement. The joint capsule is a tough fibrous sleeve enclosing the whole joint. Inside it, the synovial membrane produces synovial fluid — a viscous liquid that lubricates and delivers nutrients to the articular cartilage. Articular cartilage (hyaline cartilage) coats the bone surfaces, reducing friction and absorbing compressive forces during impact. Ligaments are strong bands of connective tissue that hold bone to bone, preventing dislocation. Some joints also contain bursae (fluid-filled sacs) to cushion areas of friction, and in the knee, fibrocartilage menisci deepen the joint surface and distribute load.

The Muscular System

There are three types of muscle tissue in the body. Cardiac muscle is found only in the heart and contracts involuntarily and continuously throughout life. Smooth muscle lines internal organs such as blood vessels and the digestive tract and also works involuntarily. Skeletal (voluntary) muscle is attached to bones via tendons and is under conscious control — it is the type of muscle used in all voluntary sporting movements.

The major voluntary muscles you must locate are: biceps (front of upper arm — flexes the elbow), triceps (rear of upper arm — extends the elbow), deltoids (top of the shoulder — abducts the arm), pectorals/pectoralis major (chest — adducts and rotates the arm), abdominals (abdomen — flex the trunk and stabilise the core), quadriceps (front of the thigh — extends the knee), hamstrings (rear of the thigh — flexes the knee), gastrocnemius (calf — plantarflexes the ankle), gluteals/gluteus maximus (buttocks — extends and externally rotates the hip), and latissimus dorsi (broad muscle of the back — pulls the arm downward and backward). The spec also includes trapezius (upper back and neck — elevates and retracts the scapula).

Key Fact

The major muscle groups are: biceps, triceps, deltoids, pectorals, abdominals, quadriceps, hamstrings, gastrocnemius, gluteus maximus, latissimus dorsi and trapezius. For each one, know its location on the body.

Muscle Fibre Types

Skeletal muscle fibres are not all identical. The specification distinguishes two main types. Type I (slow-twitch) fibres contract slowly, generate less force but are very resistant to fatigue. They are rich in mitochondria and myoglobin, giving them a red appearance, and they rely predominantly on aerobic respiration. They are well suited to endurance activities such as marathon running or cycling. Type II (fast-twitch) fibres contract rapidly and generate greater force but fatigue quickly. They rely more on anaerobic respiration and are recruited during high-intensity, short-duration activities such as sprinting or weightlifting.

The Cardiovascular System

The cardiovascular system consists of the heart, blood vessels and blood. The heart is a four-chambered pump located in the chest cavity, slightly left of centre. The right atrium receives deoxygenated blood from the body via the vena cava. From there it passes through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, which pumps it to the lungs via the pulmonary artery. Oxygenated blood returns from the lungs through the pulmonary vein into the left atrium, then passes through the mitral (bicuspid) valve into the left ventricle — the most powerful chamber — which pumps blood around the entire body through the aorta. The left ventricle has much thicker walls than the right because it must generate higher pressure for systemic circulation.

Blood travels through three types of vessel. Arteries carry blood away from the heart at high pressure; their thick, elastic walls absorb the surge of pressure from each heartbeat. Veins carry blood back towards the heart at low pressure; they have thinner walls and contain valves to prevent backflow. Capillaries are microscopic, single-cell-thick vessels that form networks within tissues, allowing the exchange of oxygen, carbon dioxide and nutrients between the blood and cells. Blood itself is composed of red blood cells (carry oxygen via haemoglobin), white blood cells (immune defence), platelets (clotting) and plasma (the liquid carrying nutrients and waste).

Arteries have three distinct wall layers: a tough outer adventitia, a thick middle layer of smooth muscle and elastic tissue (tunica media), and a smooth inner endothelium. This construction allows them to expand and recoil with each heartbeat (the pulse you feel at your wrist is an artery). Veins share the same three layers but their tunica media is much thinner — they operate at low pressure and rely on skeletal muscle contractions and one-way valves to return blood to the heart. Capillaries are just one cell thick (endothelium only), with no muscle or connective tissue layers. Their tiny diameter (7–10 micrometres) means red blood cells pass through in single file, maximising contact time with surrounding cells for efficient gas and nutrient exchange.

The Respiratory System

The respiratory system draws oxygen into the body and expels carbon dioxide. Air enters through the nose and mouth and passes down the larynx (voice box) into the trachea (windpipe), a rigid tube kept open by C-shaped rings of cartilage. At the base of the trachea the airway divides into the left and right bronchi (singular: bronchus), each leading into its respective lung. Inside each lung the bronchi branch repeatedly into progressively narrower bronchioles, ending in tiny air sacs called alveoli.

The alveoli are the functional units of gas exchange: their enormous combined surface area (approximately 70 m² in an adult), moist thin walls and rich capillary network allow oxygen to diffuse from air into blood and carbon dioxide to diffuse from blood into air. The two lungs sit within the ribcage; the right lung has three lobes and the left lung has two (to accommodate the heart). Breathing itself is driven by the diaphragm — a dome-shaped sheet of skeletal muscle beneath the lungs. When it contracts and flattens, it increases thoracic volume, drawing air in (inspiration). When it relaxes and rises back, thoracic volume decreases, forcing air out (expiration). The intercostal muscles between the ribs assist this process by lifting and lowering the ribcage.
exam_tip_html: Structural questions often ask you to name a specific part of a body system or to label a diagram. Learn the correct anatomical terms from the required list — for example, write "vena cava" not "large vein into the heart", and "gastrocnemius" not "calf muscle". For joint questions, always state the joint type and give an example location. For questions about the heart, remember the direction of blood flow: body → right atrium → right ventricle → lungs → left atrium → left ventricle → body. Drawing and labelling this pathway from memory is an excellent revision strategy.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The skeletal system consists of 206 bones, classified as long, short, flat or irregular; the main bones run from cranium to fibula. Synovial joints (ball and socket, hinge, pivot) allow free movement and share a common structure of capsule, synovial membrane, articular cartilage and ligaments.
  • The major voluntary muscles include the biceps, triceps, deltoids, pectorals, abdominals, quadriceps, hamstrings, gastrocnemius, gluteus maximus, latissimus dorsi and trapezius. Muscle fibres are either Type I (slow-twitch, aerobic, fatigue-resistant) or Type II (fast-twitch, anaerobic, powerful but fatigable).
  • The heart has four chambers (right atrium, right ventricle, left atrium, left ventricle); blood flows through arteries, capillaries and veins, and blood is composed of red cells, white cells, platelets and plasma.
  • The respiratory system moves air through the trachea, bronchi, bronchioles and into the alveoli where gas exchange takes place; breathing is controlled by the diaphragm and intercostal muscles.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of a ball and socket joint?
A) The knee
B) The elbow
C) The shoulder
D) The wrist
State two major voluntary muscles found in the lower body.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: quadriceps / hamstrings / gastrocnemius / gluteus maximus. Answers must name a muscle from the required list to score. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the structure of the trachea and explain why this structure is important during exercise.
practice_questions.marks: Description (1 mark): the trachea is a tube running from the larynx that divides into the bronchi, held open by C-shaped rings of cartilage. Explanation (up to 2 marks): the cartilage rings keep the airway open even when the neck moves during exercise, ensuring a constant flow of air to the lungs (1 mark for stating the cartilage keeps the airway open; 2 marks for adding that this prevents collapse under the pressure changes of vigorous breathing). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the journey of blood through the four chambers of the heart, naming the key blood vessels involved.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for each of the following, to a maximum of 4: deoxygenated blood enters the right atrium via the vena cava; passes into the right ventricle; is pumped to the lungs via the pulmonary artery; returns oxygenated to the left atrium via the pulmonary vein; passes into the left ventricle; is pumped to the body via the aorta. (Award up to 4 of these marks; a complete, ordered response scores 4 marks.) [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: A 16-year-old football player is told by her coach that her explosive sprinting is linked to her muscle fibre composition. Using your knowledge of muscle fibre types, explain how the structure of Type I and Type II fibres makes them suited to different sporting demands.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Detailed explanation of both fibre types with structural reasons linked clearly to sporting demands. For example: Type I (slow-twitch) fibres are rich in mitochondria and myoglobin, enabling sustained aerobic energy production — well suited to endurance activities such as a goalkeeper's repeated repositioning or a midfielder's 90-minute work rate. Type II (fast-twitch) fibres lack high mitochondrial density but have rapid cross-bridge cycling and access to large anaerobic energy stores, enabling explosive short bursts such as a sprint to the ball. The answer links structural features (mitochondria, contraction speed) to function and gives sporting examples.
Secure (3-4 marks): Both types identified and their general characteristics described, with some link to sport.
Developing (2 marks): One type described with limited sporting link.
Emerging (1 mark): A basic statement about fast and slow fibres with no structural detail. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: A sport scientist is assessing two athletes: a long-distance runner and a javelin thrower. Using your knowledge of the structure of the skeletal, muscular and cardiovascular systems, evaluate how the structural features of these systems combine to support performance in each athlete's chosen sport.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): A balanced, system-linked evaluation covering all three systems for both athlete types. For the distance runner: dense capillary networks around Type I fibres maximise oxygen delivery; synovial joints (especially hinge joints at the knee) allow repetitive extension-flexion without dislocation; long bones of the lower limb act as efficient levers; the heart's left ventricle pumps blood continuously to working muscles. For the javelin thrower: upper-body muscles (deltoids, pectorals, triceps, latissimus dorsi) generate the throwing force; ball and socket joint at the shoulder permits the circumduction needed for the run-up and release; Type II fibres in the throwing arm produce rapid, powerful contractions; the cardiovascular system recovers between throws. Substantiated conclusion about why neither athlete could perform without the integration of all three systems.
Secure (5-6 marks): At least two systems addressed for both athletes, with relevant structural points and some evaluation.
Developing (3-4 marks): Points largely descriptive; limited cross-system links.
Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic recall of individual structures with no evaluation or athlete application. [8 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Which type of synovial joint is found at the shoulder and hip, allowing movement in all planes?
Which chamber of the heart pumps oxygenated blood into the aorta to supply the whole body?
The _____ is the dome-shaped sheet of skeletal muscle beneath the lungs; when it contracts, it increases thoracic volume and draws air in during inspiration.
Type _____ muscle fibres are slow-twitch, highly resistant to fatigue and suited to aerobic endurance activities.
Match each blood vessel type to its correct structural description.
right: Thin-walled vessels containing valves that return blood to the heart at low pressure
Microscopic, single-cell-thick vessels where gas and nutrient exchange occurs
Thick, elastic, muscular vessels that carry blood away from the heart at high pressure

flashcard_questions.q: What type of bone is the femur, acting as a lever during movement?
Which bone in the upper arm connects the shoulder to the elbow?

flashcard_questions.a: A freely moveable joint with a capsule and synovial fluid for lubrication.

flashcard_questions.q: Which synovial joint type allows movement in all planes, found at the shoulder and hip?
Which muscle extends the knee during a kicking action?
What is the difference between Type I and Type II muscle fibres?
flashcard_questions.a: Type I: slow-twitch, fatigue-resistant, aerobic. Type II: fast-twitch, powerful, fatigues quickly.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the four chambers of the heart in order of blood flow.
flashcard_questions.a: Right atrium, right ventricle, left atrium, left ventricle.

flashcard_questions.q: What vessel carries deoxygenated blood from the body into the heart?
How do arteries differ from veins in structure?
flashcard_questions.a: Arteries have thick elastic walls; veins have thin walls with valves.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the role of the alveoli in the respiratory system?
flashcard_questions.a: Gas exchange: oxygen diffuses into blood; carbon dioxide diffuses out.

flashcard_questions.q: Which muscle is the prime mover of inspiration?
Where is the gastrocnemius muscle located and what does it do?
flashcard_questions.a: The calf; it plantarflexes the ankle, powering push-off in running and jumping.

glossary_terms.definition: A group of organs and tissues that work together to carry out a specific function in the body.
The point at which two or more bones meet; in synovial joints, the joint is freely moveable and lubricated by synovial fluid.
Slow-twitch muscle fibres that are highly resistant to fatigue, rely on aerobic respiration and are recruited for low-intensity, long-duration activities such as distance running.
Blood vessels that carry oxygenated blood away from the heart to the body's tissues; they have thick, elastic, muscular walls to withstand high pressure.
The airway running from the larynx to the bronchi; a rigid tube held open by C-shaped rings of cartilage.
